title: Give and invite (Avot 5:13)
hook: one who gives and wants others to give too has a good eye
tomorrow: a whole page of notes: which ones do you keep?

segments.voice: Yesterday, slow to anger: slow in, quick out, and beside it a neighbor's line, swift to hear. Today closes the week, with a question about giving.

A fundraiser link lands in the group chat: a food drive, a friend's surgery, a school's costume fund. You give, quietly. Then the question: do you post it and ask everyone else? To some people that sounds like showing off. Is it bragging to ask others to give too? Avot has a four-way answer, and the surprise is who gets called stingy.
screen: `A LINK IN THE GROUP CHAT.` → `YOU GIVE, QUIETLY.` → `THEN: ASK EVERYONE ELSE?`

segments.voice: Avot 5:13 sorts givers of tzedakah four ways. One wants to give, but doesn't want others to: that one's eye is bad toward what belongs to others. One wants others to give, but won't: a bad eye toward their own. One gives and wants others to give: a chasid. One neither gives nor wants anyone else to: wicked. The surprise is the first. Giving alone and keeping the field to yourself gets called a bad eye: begrudging other people their own good deed. So in Avot's terms, inviting others isn't bragging. It's part of the gift. Now the round, because this is the week's end. Erased paper takes ink: both still write. You didn't choose the frame: given, and still accountable. A world made with ten sayings, so each life weighs. Tongs and a rainbow, made at twilight. Three honest words: I have not heard. And the chasid's temper, slow to anger. Line them up and a pattern shows. Almost every saying this week is about what you do with what you were handed: a used page, an unchosen life, a careful world, a blank, a hot moment, a gift.
screen: `FOUR KINDS OF GIVERS.` · `THE BAD EYE: GIVING ALONE.` · `THE WEEK'S ROUND.` · `WHAT YOU DO WITH WHAT YOU'RE HANDED.` · then, large: `GIVE AND INVITE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who gives, time, food, money, attention, and rarely hears about it. Write them a short message that names the thing they do, plainly, in a sentence or two. Send it if it feels right; keep it as a draft if not.
screen: `SOMEONE WHO GIVES.` · `NAME WHAT THEY DO.` · `SEND IT, OR KEEP IT.`

segments.voice: Give and invite: Avot's chasid gives, and wants others to give too. The giving makes room.
The week's last line: give and invite, and let others have their good deed too. Week done; see you on the other side.

howItsDone: Tzedakah is a duty in Jewish law, and communities often give together: a tzedakah box at home or school, a collective appeal, or friends pooling gifts for someone in need.

myth: in Avot, the wise never say 'I don't know'
the wise one says 'I have not heard' about what they haven't heard.
Avot faults the one who gives but doesn't want others to give
their eye is bad toward what belongs to others: they begrudge others the good deed.

fork.setup: a coworker loves organizing donation drives but never puts anything in himself. which of Avot's four givers is he?
options: a bad eye toward his own: he wants others to give, but not himself.
the chasid: getting others to give counts the same as giving.
the wicked one: he neither gives nor wants others to give.
fork.reveal: Avot names him: wants others to give, but won't himself. the chasid does both: gives, and invites.

original.note: Hebrew: a person of devotion; in Avot 5:13, one who gives and wants others to give.

trapdoor: what you thought: asking others to give is showing off.
what it means: Avot calls the one who gives and wants others to give a chasid.
what a scholar hears: the 'bad eye' is begrudging: the lone giver begrudges others their merit; the one who only asks begrudges his own money.
guess: giving, and urging others to give too
giving only after others have given
a gift that is handed back to the giver
recall: a world made with care: it all weighs
honest about what you haven't learned

chat.meaning: In Avot 5:13 the one who gives and wants others to give is a chasid; giving alone and begrudging others is a bad eye.

Avot 5:13 paraphrased: four types among givers of tzedakah: wants to give but not that others give, his eye is evil toward what is others'; that others give but not he, his eye is evil toward what is his; he gives and others give, chasid; neither, wicked. The index hook says 'good eye'; the mishnah's words for this case are 'chasid'. Script uses chasid and explains the 'bad eye' of the other cases. Confirm.
